kurz: Why the thesis about the internet was right and the price of dotcom shares was wrong nonetheless, and why this case is the hardest to recognise.

bloecke.md:
On 9 August 1995, Netscape went public. The issue price was $28 and the closing price on the first trading day around $58, although the company made no significant profit. Just under eight years later, on 5 June 2003, Deutsche Börse closed the Neuer Markt, its segment for growth companies. In between lies the most instructive case in recent financial history, because everything essential can be observed in it at the same time: a thesis that turned out to be right, prices that were wrong nonetheless, a stock exchange segment with its own rules that mainly attracted companies which would not have met stricter rules, and analysts whose work was financed by the underwriting business.

The internet has changed the world. That was already in every prospectus in 1999 and was essentially true, so it is not an insight gained in hindsight. The forecast about the technology was right. What was wrong was the amount investors paid in advance for it to come true.

## Capital inflows and interest rate policy

On 5 December 1996, Alan Greenspan publicly asked whether prices were an expression of “irrational exuberance”. The Nasdaq Composite stood at around 1,300 points at the time. By its peak of 5,048.62 points on 10 March 2000, it had risen almost fourfold. The warning was right, but came three years too early. Investors who heeded it initially missed this rise. In October 2002, however, the index stood at around 1,114 points, below its level of December 1996.

The final phase of the rise was helped by a rescue operation that had nothing to do with technology. After the Russian default of August 1998 and the collapse of the hedge fund LTCM, the Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate in three steps from 5.50% to 4.75% within seven weeks. Over the following sixteen months, the Nasdaq rose once more to around 2.7 times its level. Only from June 1999 did the Fed raise interest rates again. By the time the index reached its peak, it had raised its key interest rate four times, to 5.75%. Two further steps to 6.50% followed afterwards.

bloecke.titel: The Fed's key interest rate during the dotcom bubble
bloecke.unter: The rate cuts in autumn 1998 fell in the final phase of the rise, and the eleven cuts of 2001 did not stop the crash.

bloecke.md:
## The Neuer Markt

The German version started on 10 March 1997. For the Nemax All Share and the better-known selection index Nemax 50, which was only added on 1 July 1999, a base of 1,000 points as of 30 December 1997 applies. The segment's rules demanded more than the rest of the market, namely quarterly reports, international accounting standards and lock-up periods for founders' shares. Nevertheless, accounting scandals piled up on the Neuer Markt. At ComROAD, the reported revenue was almost entirely invented, and EM.TV and Infomatec are further cases of this kind. The accumulation had a systematic cause. A new segment that sets out to raise capital for companies without a profit history lowers the entry barrier for everyone, including companies for which the barrier would have served its purpose.

Over 300 companies were listed. The Nemax 50 reached 9,666 points on 10 March 2000, the same day as the Nasdaq, and fell to 318 points by 9 October 2002. Around €200 billion of market value was lost. Private investors were also hit outside the segment. The third tranche of the Deutsche Telekom share (T-Aktie) was issued in June 2000 at €66.50, and two years later the share was trading below ten euros.

bloecke.titel: Decline and recovery of four indices

bloecke.md: The values in the “Rise needed” column follow from simple fractions. An index that falls from 9,666 to 318 stands at 3.3% of its starting value and has to increase thirtyfold to get back. Two figures circulate for the DAX peak: 8,064.97 points on a closing basis and 8,136.16 points intraday. When comparing drawdowns, that is, declines from the peak, the basis must therefore be stated, otherwise you end up comparing figures that measure different things. For the DAX, the table uses closing prices.

## Valuation without profits

For a company without profits, the price-to-earnings ratio is undefined rather than high. The bubble in the narrower sense began when this usual ratio was replaced because it did not yield a number. Its place was taken by the sales multiple, user numbers, page views and the burn rate, that is, the capital consumed each month, which was reinterpreted as investment in growth. For the Nasdaq as a whole, insofar as it reported profits, the P/E was about 200 at the end of 1999. That was more than double the P/E of around 80 at the height of the Japanese bubble.

bloecke.formel: Sales multiple = Market capitalisation ÷ Annual revenue
bloecke.erklaerung: The multiple is correct in itself, but it assumes a margin that it does not show. Two companies with the same revenue and the same market value get the same ratio, even if one achieves a margin of 5% and the other 30%.
variablen: share price × total number of shares
revenue over the last twelve months, before all costs

bloecke.md:
Suppose a company is valued at ten times its annual revenue, and the shareholders want to get the purchase price back within ten years.

Then the company would have to pay out its entire revenue to the shareholders for ten years. Nothing would be left for production costs, salaries, research, taxes and investment in growth, and revenue could not fall in any of those ten years.

A calculation with a permanent net margin of 10% is more realistic. A sales multiple of 10 then corresponds to a P/E of 100. In this case, the price contains the assumption that revenue and margin will both rise strongly over many years. That is possible, but it also has to happen for the purchase at the entry price to pay off.

## Analysts' conflicts of interest

The analysts at the big banks were not independent. They were part of a business model in which research was cross-subsidised by the underwriting business. At the same time, a company rarely awards the mandate for its IPO to a bank whose analyst is currently recommending selling. Sell recommendations therefore made up only a vanishingly small share of all ratings.

This was only dealt with after the crash. In April 2003, ten large US banks reached a settlement with the SEC, the state securities regulators and other authorities: the Global Research Analyst Settlement. It provided for payments of around $1.4 billion and the organisational separation of research and underwriting. In addition, two of the most prominent analysts, the internet analyst Henry Blodget and the telecoms analyst Jack Grubman, were barred from the industry for life. In the EU, Article 20 of the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/958 now apply. Under these rules, persons who disseminate investment recommendations must disclose their interests and conflicts of interest. In Germany, Section 85 WpHG (Securities Trading Act) supplements these obligations. Disclosure only makes the conflict visible and does not remove it. Readers still have to check for themselves who paid for a recommendation.

## How the decline unfolded

Bubbles rarely burst on a single day. The decline lasted 31 months and was interrupted by recovery phases that each time looked like the end of the fall. The Fed cut its key interest rate eleven times in 2001, from 6.50% to 1.75%, yet the Nasdaq continued to fall that year. On 11 September 2001, the DAX lost 8.49% in one day. The accounting scandal at Enron came to light in the autumn of 2001, the one at Worldcom in June 2002, and prices only reached their low on 9 October 2002.

In the DAX, the loss was spread over three calendar years: −7.54% in 2000, −19.79% in 2001 and −43.94% in 2002, the worst year in the history of the DAX. Taken together, the three annual returns come to around −58%, whereas the decline from peak to low was around −73%. The difference arises because the peak in March 2000 and the low in March 2003 did not fall at a year end. The three annual returns run from the end of 1999 to the end of 2002 and capture neither the rise to the peak nor the further decline to the low. Dividends do not explain the difference, because both figures come from the same performance index.

bloecke.titel: DAX annual returns in the three loss years
bloecke.unter: The worst year came last, two and a half years after the peak. Bubbles unwind so slowly that at times the decline credibly seems to be over.

bloecke.md:
Around 48% of the dotcom companies still existed in 2004, albeit at much lower valuations. Amazon and eBay were genuine winners. Yet even Amazon lost over 90% of its market value, Cisco around 80%, and Pets.com closed nine months after its IPO.

Investors who conclude from the example of Amazon that holding on pays off are picking their evidence in hindsight from the group of survivors. By the same rule, in 1999 you would have invested with equal conviction in several hundred companies that no longer exist today. An index can recover because it removes insolvent companies and adds successful ones. In a portfolio of individual shares, this does not happen by itself.

bloecke.titel: Thesis and price as separate decisions
bloecke.unter: The dotcom bubble was in the top right. The technology arrived, but the entry price had already anticipated it. Returns, by contrast, are made in the top left.

felder.text: The rare case. Internet stocks in 2002/03, when the same business models could be had for a fraction of the price.
The dotcom case. The forecast comes true, the return does not, because the price anticipated it.
Limited damage. Little expectation in the price, so little room to fall if it fails to materialise.
The total loss. ComROAD and the companies without revenue belong here.

bloecke.md: A forecast about a technology and a forecast about returns are two different statements. The second includes the price, and only the price determines how much of a correct thesis reaches the investor.

## Tax treatment of the losses

Investors who sold at a loss in 2002 were subject to legal rules that no longer exist. Before the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), price gains were only taxable within the one-year speculation period (Spekulationsfrist) under Section 23 EStG (Income Tax Act) in the version then in force. After a holding period of more than one year, a loss could not be claimed for tax purposes at all. Because gains were tax-free in this case, losses conversely had no effect either. For a sale within the period, the loss could only be offset against gains from other private disposals.

Today, losses from capital assets may not be offset against wages, rent or business income. They are only offset within income from capital assets, but can be carried forward there without limit (Section 20(6) sentences 1 to 3 EStG). There is still a separate loss pot (Verlusttopf) for shares. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from share sales, not against dividends, interest or ETF gains (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). According to the BMF circular of 14 May 2025 (para. 118), this also applies to losses on shares that are derecognised as worthless. Only losses that a bank still recorded under the old law up to its system changeover go into the general loss pot, for reasons of simplification. Banks must apply this allocation when withholding tax from 1 January 2026 at the latest (para. 325). For tax purposes, an insolvency is thus treated exactly like a timely emergency sale.

- Before buying any growth share, you should be clear about which development in revenue and margin must occur for today's price to work out. Without this answer, the purchase rests only on the story told about the company.
- Risk is better managed through position size than through the timing of the exit. Greenspan's warning came three years too early. Investors who consider a theme expensive can reduce its weighting, because hitting the turning point is not a realistic goal.
- You should know the loss pots before you need them. If you have securities accounts at several banks, losses at bank A are not automatically offset against gains at bank B. This requires a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung) under Section 43a(3) sentences 4 and 5 EStG, which must be applied for irrevocably by 15 December of the year. In addition, FIFO is mandatory when you sell (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG).

bloecke.unter: More than three years passed between the first official warning and the peak, and 31 months between the peak and the low.

bloecke.md:
Depending on the account, the trigger is said to have been the rate rises, an antitrust ruling against Microsoft, disappointing quarterly results or the expiry of lock-up periods, after which founders and early investors were allowed to sell for the first time.

All of these events were small compared with what followed, and that is typical. The trigger is the occasion on which market participants correct their expectations. The potential fall, that is, the extent of the possible price decline, builds up beforehand. It results from the price, from the share of unprofitable companies in the index and from the willingness to justify valuations with substitute metrics. Examining the triggers therefore mainly yields a chronology. For risk management, the potential fall is more revealing.

Unlike purely financial manias, this one left real assets behind. The fibre-optic lines laid in the boom years and the server capacity that had been built up remained available even after their builders went bankrupt, at a fraction of the construction costs. In economic terms, the bubble was therefore more productive than its reputation. For the builders' shareholders, it nevertheless meant a total loss. The investors' loss of capital and the successors' gain in capacity stem from the same process.

mitnehmen: The technology thesis of the dotcom era was right; the losses arose from the price at which investors bought into it.
If there are no profits, the valuation ratio is replaced, and substitute measures such as sales multiples and user numbers do not reveal the margin.
A loss of 96.7% requires a rise of 2,940%, so it is more valuable to avoid a large potential fall than to hit the low.
The crash lasted 31 months with several convincing-looking interim recoveries, and even eleven rate cuts in 2001 did not stop it.
Citing Amazon and eBay as evidence that holding on pays off is a selection made in hindsight, because around half of the companies had disappeared by 2004.

begriffe.text: Market capitalisation divided by annual revenue. For companies without profits, the ratio serves as a substitute for the P/E. Because it ignores the margin, it is only as meaningful as the later profitability that is assumed.
Amount by which a company's monthly spending exceeds its income. The burn rate and the liquid funds together show how much time remains until the next funding round.
